subject: community-medicine
title: Disaster Management: Cycle, Triage, NDMA, and Post Disaster Surveillance

steps.title: The disaster management cycle
steps.tx: The **disaster management cycle** organises action into response, rehabilitation, reconstruction, prevention, mitigation, and preparedness, looping continuously rather than ending at relief. A disaster is an event overwhelming local capacity (WHO phrasing), whether sudden (earthquake, flood, chemical leak) or slow (drought, famine). The cycle's lesson for health managers: most lives are saved by preparedness bought years before the sirens.
steps.say: Response, recovery, mitigation, preparedness: the cycle never stops. Preparedness purchased early saves the most lives.

steps.title: Mitigation versus preparedness
steps.tx: Two pre disaster words divide cleanly in **mitigation and preparedness in disasters**: mitigation reduces the hazard's damage potential permanently (embankments, earthquake resistant codes, land use zoning), while preparedness readies response (mock drills, stockpiles, hospital disaster plans, trained teams). Insurance and early warning systems straddle both. Examination stems describing building codes want mitigation; describing drills want preparedness.
steps.say: Mitigation rebuilds the world safer; preparedness rehearses the response. Codes mitigate, drills prepare.

steps.title: Triage colour coding
steps.tx: At a mass casualty scene, **triage colour coding** sorts victims by survival urgency under scarcity: red for immediate (airway, breathing, bleeding threats salvageable now), yellow for delayed (serious but stable hours), green for minimal (walking wounded), and black for deceased or expectant (unsalvageable with available resources). The ethical inversion (treat the salvageable urgent before the moribund) defines disaster medicine against ordinary queue ethics.
steps.say: Red now, yellow later, green walking, black expectant. Disaster triage treats salvageable urgency first, not first come.

steps.title: START triage in sixty seconds
steps.tx: **START triage (Simple Triage And Rapid Treatment)** classifies adults in under a minute each: can they walk (green), then breathing (absent after airway opening: black; above thirty: red), perfusion (capillary refill or radial pulse), and mental status (follows commands or not). JumpSTART adapts the algorithm for children, whose respiratory physiology inverts adult priorities. Speed with acceptable accuracy beats precision that arrives after death.
steps.say: Walk, breathe, perfuse, obey: START sorts in sixty seconds. Children get the JumpSTART respiratory first variant.

steps.title: Mass casualty management chain
steps.tx: **Mass casualty management** chains scene triage to casualty clearing, graded transport, and hospital surge: incident command assigns roles, hospitals activate disaster plans (recall staff, clear beds, postpone electives), and a single medical control coordinates destinations so the nearest hospital is not drowned while others idle. Communication failure, not clinical skill, is the usual system fracture in after action reviews.
steps.say: Command, triage, staged transport, hospital surge. Most disaster failures are communication failures wearing clinical clothes.

steps.title: NDMA and the Disaster Management Act 2005
steps.tx: India's **Disaster Management Act 2005** created the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA, chaired by the Prime Minister), state and district authorities, the National Disaster Response Force, and dedicated funds, shifting policy from relief distribution to prevention, mitigation, and preparedness. The National Disaster Management Plan (2016) aligns agencies and explicitly adopts the Sendai framework priorities for Indian conditions.
steps.say: The 2005 Act built NDMA under the Prime Minister and a response force. Policy moved from relief to prevention.

steps.title: Sendai Framework priorities
steps.tx: The **Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015 to 2030)** succeeded the Hyogo framework with four priorities: understand disaster risk, strengthen risk governance, invest in resilience, and enhance preparedness with build back better recovery, against seven global targets including mortality and affected people reduction. Its risk reduction (not just response) philosophy is the sentence examinations reward candidates for reproducing.
steps.say: Sendai 2015 to 2030: understand risk, govern it, invest against it, build back better. Risk reduction outranks response.

steps.title: Post disaster surveillance and epidemics
steps.tx: After floods and earthquakes, **post disaster disease surveillance** watches for diarrhoea, acute respiratory infection, leptospirosis, malaria, measles in camps, and wound infections through daily syndromic reporting from relief sites, with safe water, sanitation, and vector control as the true prevention. Contrary to myth, corpses of disaster victims rarely cause epidemics; crowding, water failure, and interrupted immunisation do.
steps.say: Watch water, crowding, and camps, not corpses, for post disaster epidemics. Syndromic daily reporting catches the real threats.

steps.title: Man made disasters and NDMA guidelines
steps.tx: **Man made disasters** (chemical Bhopal pattern, industrial fires, nuclear and radiological events, transport crashes, stampedes) demand hazard specific plans: chemical antidote stockpiles and decontamination corridors, burn surge capacity, radiation monitoring, and crowd management science. NDMA issues subject guidelines for each hazard family, and district plans must localise them with hospital and industry liaison before the event, never during it.
steps.say: Chemical, fire, nuclear, crowd: each man made hazard needs its own rehearsed plan. Bhopal wrote that lesson in 1984.
